practicalQuestion: What should pre-training fueling and hydration prioritize for a collegiate athlete completing an early-morning high-intensity session when appetite is low and less than 45 minutes are available before training?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate athletes participating in high-intensity morning training
decisionContext.phase: Before an early-morning field or court session
decisionContext.outcome: Support session quality with a practical, tolerable intake approach
decisionContext.constraints: Low appetite; limited preparation time; individual gastrointestinal tolerance; no clinical nutrition condition

evidenceConfidence.rationale: No primary study in the pack tests carbohydrate or fluid intake within 45 minutes of training, with low appetite, or with pre-exercise gut tolerance as an outcome. The short-window guidance available comes from reviews: a rugby league match-day table suggests a light snack or drink 30 to 60 minutes before if hungry, and a caffeine review summarizes trials that gave caffeine 5 to 60 minutes before testing. Carbohydrate evidence comes from professional male rugby league and a two-player Australian Football case report. Hydration evidence comes from male high school and post-graduate American football players in hot or warm pre-season practices. Caffeine benefits in actual team-sport matches are inconsistent. These sources inform options but do not support choosing one approach for this situation.

dimensions.sourceReview: Two narrative reviews (rugby league nutrition; caffeine and sleep), one two-player case report on muscle glycogen, one field study of 31 high school football players, one smart-bottle validation study in 30 football players, and one editorial on football (soccer) in the heat.
dimensions.directness: Indirect. No primary study examines intake under 45 minutes before training, low appetite, or food form and gut tolerance before exercise. Short-window suggestions exist only as review-level guidance: a rugby league match-day table (light snack or drink 30 to 60 minutes prematch if hungry) and caffeine trials summarized in a review (5 to 60 minutes before testing).
dimensions.consistency: Sources broadly agree that high-intensity team-sport work is thought to rely on carbohydrate availability and that hydration needs are individual. Caffeine benefits in team-sport matches are mixed across studies. Measurement evidence on pre-practice urine markers is mixed.
dimensions.transferability: Carbohydrate guidance comes from professional male rugby league and elite male Australian Football; hydration data come from male high school and post-graduate American football players. The caffeine review covers athletes of both sexes and reports similar caffeine benefits in men and women, but not in collegiate samples. No source studied a collegiate morning team-sport session with a short pre-training window, and no carbohydrate or hydration source studied women.

bottomLine.text: No primary study in the library tests what to eat or drink in the last 45 minutes before an early session when appetite is low. Review-level guidance offers options: a rugby league match-day table suggests lower-fiber carbohydrate closer to kickoff and a light snack or drink 30 to 60 minutes before if hungry; caffeine trials used 3 to 6 mg/kg, typically within 60 minutes, and morning use is less likely to disturb that night's sleep. High-intensity team-sport play is thought to rely heavily on muscle glycogen, and hydration status varies widely between athletes and is hard to judge from urine alone.

actions.title: Option: move carbohydrate earlier
actions.text: In a two-player case report, a 24-hour carbohydrate-loading protocol plus a prematch meal 4 hours before play raised muscle glycogen, and a rugby league review emphasizes high carbohydrate availability for key sessions. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): when the morning window is short, the prior day and evening meal may carry more of the fueling load than the pre-session snack.

actions.title: Option: a small, low-fiber intake in the window if tolerated
actions.text: A rugby league review's match-day table suggests 1 to 4 g/kg carbohydrate 1 to 4 hours before, lower-fiber (high GI) choices closer to kickoff, and a light snack or drink after the warm-up 30 to 60 minutes before if hungry. These are suggestions for professional male rugby league matches, not tested in morning training or in athletes with low appetite. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): any small intake should be trialed in training first.

actions.title: Option: caffeine for athletes who already use it
actions.text: The caffeine review reports a recommendation of about 3 to 6 mg/kg about 1 hour before exercise, but also summarizes trials that gave caffeine 5 to 60 minutes before testing and an ISSN recommendation of within 60 minutes; the rugby league review suggests 30 to 60 minutes before matches. The review cites earlier work that gum is absorbed faster than capsules, and reports similar benefits in men and women. Morning use is less likely to disrupt that night's sleep. Responses vary between athletes, gastrointestinal problems are a listed side effect, and benefits in actual team-sport matches have been inconsistent. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): confirm dose and product against institutional and governing-body rules and sports dietitian guidance, and trial in training before use.

actions.title: Option: start from an individual hydration baseline
actions.text: Fluid balance in early-morning post-graduate football practices ranged from a 2.35% loss to a 0.47% gain across athletes, and Ashley and colleagues cite a study of NCAA athletes in which 66% arrived at practice with urine specific gravity indicating hypohydration. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): fluid intake before the session can be set per athlete rather than as one team volume.

monitoring.label: Hydration status with more than one measure
monitoring.text: In 31 high school football players, neither urine color nor urine specific gravity alone validly detected 2% or greater body mass loss, although few values reached that level; urine color did track urine specific gravity well. The authors suggest multiple assessments may help reduce misclassification.

monitoring.label: Back-to-back sessions
monitoring.text: Urine color carryover was greater when practices were less than 24 hours apart, and body mass loss was greatest after 2-a-day practices or a morning practice after an evening practice, although body mass suggested athletes rehydrated between practices. Watch athletes whose morning session follows a session the evening before.

monitoring.label: Tolerance and session quality
monitoring.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): log gut comfort, appetite, and perceived session quality for any pre-session intake or caffeine trial, since the cited reviews stress individual response, list gastrointestinal problems among caffeine side effects, and advise players to trial strategies.

guardrails.text: Carbohydrate doses and timings in the pack are match-day suggestions for professional male rugby league players, and caffeine doses come from trials across sports. Do not apply them as fixed targets for a collegiate sub-45-minute morning window.

If the session is in heat, an editorial on football (soccer) in the heat, citing earlier work, treats staying euhydrated during a match as essential, which raises the importance of the hydration options above.

limitations.text: No primary study in the pack tested pre-training carbohydrate or fluid intake within 45 minutes, low morning appetite, or gut tolerance before exercise. Short-window guidance comes from a review table for rugby league matches and a review summarizing caffeine trials timed 5 to 60 minutes before testing.
Glycogen data come from a case report of 2 elite male Australian Football forwards in a match, not a morning training session, and only one player consumed carbohydrate during play.

Hydration studies were in male high school and post-graduate American football players during hot or warm pre-season practices, and only 11.5% of the high school players' body mass loss values exceeded 2%.

whatCouldChange.text: Trials in team-sport athletes comparing small carbohydrate or fluid intakes taken less than 45 minutes before high-intensity training, with gut tolerance measured, could support a Recommended Direction.

Studies of caffeine taken within 45 minutes of an early-morning team-sport training session in collegiate women and men, measuring session performance and gut comfort, would clarify whether the caffeine option fits this window.

evidenceTension.text: Ashley and colleagues cite a study in which 66% of NCAA athletes started practice with urine specific gravity indicating hypohydration, and in their own high school study urine color showed carryover between closely spaced practices. Yet in that same high school study, urine markers alone did not validly detect 2% or greater body mass loss, and body mass suggested athletes rehydrated between practices. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): a single pre-session urine check may over- or under-flag athletes.

claims.text: A narrative review of young professional male rugby league players suggests competition nutrition of 1 to 4 g/kg carbohydrate plus about 0.25 g/kg protein taken 1 to 4 hours before exercise for 80 to 120 kg players.

evidence.excerpt: Competition nutrition should maximize glycogen availability by consuming 1-4 g/kg carbohydrate (∼80-320 g) plus 0.25 g/kg (∼20-30 g) protein, 1-4 hr preexercise for 80-120 kg players.

claims.text: The same rugby league review suggests players may need about 6 to 8 g/kg/day carbohydrate and should target high carbohydrate availability for key training sessions and matches, while the authors note data may be insufficient for sport-specific recommendations.

evidence.excerpt: the available data suggest that players may require approximately 6-8 g·kg−1·day−1 carbohydrate, 1.6-2.6 g·kg−1·day−1 protein
Players should target high CHO availability for key training sessions and matches, possibly using “red, amber, or green” ratings corresponding to high, medium, and low CHO intake

claims.text: In a case report on elite male Australian Football, the authors state, citing earlier work, that given the 80 to 120 minute duration and high-intensity intermittent profile of team-sport match play, muscle glycogen is considered the predominant energy substrate.

evidence.excerpt: Given the duration of activity (ie, 80-120 min) and high-intensity intermittent proﬁles, muscle glycogen is considered to be the predominant energy substrate to support the metabolic demands of match play

claims.text: In that case report, 2 elite male forwards followed a 24-hour carbohydrate-loading diet of 8 g/kg plus a prematch meal of 2 g/kg carbohydrate 4 hours before a match; one player also consumed 88 g carbohydrate during play.

evidence.excerpt: After a 24-h CHO-loading protocol of 8 and 2 g/kg in the prematch meal, 2 elite male forward players had biopsies sampled from m. vastus lateralis before and after participation in a South Australian Football League game.
At 4 hours prior to match play, each player also consumed a prematch meal providing 2 g/kg CHO, 0.2 g/kg protein, and 0.3 g/kg fat.

claims.text: A narrative review reports the current caffeine recommendation as about 3 to 6 mg/kg about 1 hour before exercise.

evidence.excerpt: The current recommendation for caffeine supplementation is ingesting ~ 3-6 mg/kg about 1 h before the onset of exercise.

claims.text: The caffeine review states that, given caffeine's half-life, caffeine before a morning competition or training session can enhance performance without compromising nighttime sleep.

evidence.excerpt: consuming caffeine before a morning competition or training session can enhance performance without compromising nighttime sleep

claims.text: The caffeine review states that performance and sleep responses to caffeine vary between individuals and with session conditions, and that practitioners should assess athletes individually.

evidence.excerpt: the performance response to caffeine and the effect of this substance on sleep quality can vary interindividually and depend on the conditions of the exercise session

claims.text: Ashley and colleagues cite an earlier study of 174 NCAA athletes in various sports in which 66% had pre-practice urine specific gravity of 1.020 or higher, described as indicating hypohydration.

evidence.excerpt: In a study evaluating prepractice USG in 174 NCAA athletes in various sports, 66% of the athletes had a USG of $1.020, indicative of hypohydration

claims.text: In 31 male high school football players during hot preseason practices, neither urine color nor urine specific gravity alone was a valid measure for detecting 2% or greater body mass loss, although only 11.5% of body mass loss values exceeded 2%; the authors suggest multiple assessments may help reduce misclassification of hydration.

evidence.excerpt: The results of our subjects do not suggest that either Ucol or USG alone can be used as a valid measure of hydration to detect %BML similar to that seen in our subjects
with only 11.5% of %BML values greater than 2% across all outdoor practice days
Because no single measure of hydration status is without limitations, multiple assessments may help reduce misclassification of hydration.

claims.text: In the same high school football study, urine color carryover from post-practice to the next pre-practice was greater after the first outdoor practice and when practices were less than 24 hours apart.

evidence.excerpt: The postpractice to prepractice differences were greater after the first outdoor practice (practice 2) and for practices with less than 24 hours between practices.

claims.text: In the same study, post-practice to next pre-practice body mass did not differ meaningfully, which the authors interpret as athletes adequately rehydrating between practices.

evidence.excerpt: This suggests that athletes were able to adequately rehydrate between practices.

claims.text: In 30 male post-graduate American football players (about 18 years old) drinking ad libitum during early-morning outdoor pre-season practices in warm, humid conditions, fluid balance ranged from a 2.35% loss to a 0.47% gain.

evidence.excerpt: Fluid balance also varied substantially among athletes; ranging from 2.35% loss to 0.47% gain during the practice sessions

claims.text: An editorial on football (soccer) in the heat states, citing earlier work, that maintaining euhydration during a match in the heat is essential and can reduce internal body temperature compared with playing dehydrated.

evidence.excerpt: maintaining euhydration during a football match in the heat is essential and it can reduce internal body temperature and improve physiological function compared with playing in a dehydrated state

claims.text: The caffeine review summarizes trials that gave 2.1 to 6 mg/kg caffeine typically within 60 minutes (range 5 to 60 minutes) before testing, and reports an ISSN recommendation of 3 to 6 mg/kg within 60 minutes; the rugby league review, citing a position stand, suggests caffeine 30 to 60 minutes before matches.

evidence.excerpt: In trials, the amount of caffeine ingested varied from 2.1 mg/kg to 6 mg/kg and was typically ingested ≤ 60 min (ranging from 5 to 60 min) prior to physical tests or activities
the recommendations of the International Society of Sports Nutrition remained the same (ingestion of 3-6 mg/kg of caffeine ≤ 60 min prior to the activity)
Players could ingest caffeine 30-60 min prematch to ensure peak concentrations are achieved during matches

claims.text: In its table of suggested match-day strategies for professional male rugby league, the review advises lower-fiber (high GI) carbohydrate closer to kickoff and, 30 to 60 minutes prematch, a light snack or drink after the warm-up if hungry.

evidence.excerpt: The closer to kickoff, the lower in ﬁber (i.e., high GI) 30-60 min prematch Consume light snack/ drink after warm-up, if hungry

claims.text: The caffeine review cites earlier work that caffeine gum is absorbed faster than capsules, and states that the ergogenic effect appears to depend more on the correct individual amount than on the source.

evidence.excerpt: providing caffeine supplementation in a gum format increases the rate of absorption when compared with a capsule format
the ergogenic effect appears to be more dependent on providing the correct amount of caffeine with an individual approach rather than the source of caffeine ingestion

claims.text: The caffeine review notes, citing earlier work, that caffeine can cause side effects including nervousness, diuresis, gastrointestinal problems, and insomnia.

evidence.excerpt: Although no longer banned, caffeine consumption may elicit side effects, including nervousness, irritability, diuresis, gastrointestinal problems, and insomnia

claims.text: The caffeine review reports that earlier studies did not find reliably clear benefits during soccer, rugby, ice hockey, and basketball matches or simulated matches, while one meta-analysis of six studies found greater running and sprint distances in team sports.

evidence.excerpt: previous research has not reported reliably clear performance benefits during soccer, rugby, ice hockey, and basketball matches or simulated matches
one meta-analysis [21] identified caffeine benefits in team sport performances with players covering greater running and sprint distances

claims.text: The rugby league review advises players to trial caffeine strategies, considering preferences, the variable caffeine content of products, and variable performance responses.

evidence.excerpt: Players should trial potentially effective strategies, considering preferences and the variability of caffeine in products (5-564 mg) and performance responses

claims.text: In the high school football study, mean body mass loss was mild (0.74% to 1.48%) and was greatest when less than 24 hours separated practices, such as 2-a-day practices or a morning practice after an evening practice; the authors note increasing equipment likely also contributed.

evidence.excerpt: The practices with the greatest %BML were those after less than 24 hours between practices such as a 2-a-day practice or a morning practice after an evening practice.

claims.text: In the high school football study, urine color showed good sensitivity and specificity for identifying elevated urine specific gravity.

evidence.excerpt: Our study provides evidence of good sensitivity and specificity for using Ucol to determine USG.

claims.text: The caffeine review states, citing earlier work, that male and female athletes benefit from caffeine with similar performance magnitudes.

evidence.excerpt: Both male and female athletes benefit from caffeine supplementation with similar performance magnitudes

assumptions: Session duration, environmental temperature, and whether the athlete habitually uses caffeine were not specified; the brief assumes a non-extreme environment and treats caffeine as optional.
The athlete is assumed to have a prior-day eating opportunity that staff can influence.
coverageGaps: Primary studies (not review-level suggestions) of carbohydrate or fluid intake taken less than 45 minutes before high-intensity team-sport training
Evidence on pre-exercise fueling for athletes with low morning appetite, including food form (liquid versus solid) and gastrointestinal tolerance before exercise
Studies of fasted versus fed early-morning sessions in collegiate team-sport athletes
Pre-training carbohydrate or hydration studies in collegiate women

This brief informs practitioner judgment. It does not prescribe intake for an individual athlete. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): athletes with a clinical nutrition condition, disordered eating concerns, or persistent low appetite should be referred to a sports dietitian or physician.
